AU.title: Statement by the Monetary Policy Board: Monetary Policy Decision
AU.text:
At its meeting today, the Board decided to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to
4.85 per cent.
Inflation remains elevated and recent data indicate that it is broadly based. The inflation outlook
has also been revised materially higher in the updated staff forecasts. This partly reflects higher
fuel and other commodity prices affected by the conflict in the Middle East. But domestic capacity
pressures are also judged to have been a little tighter than earlier thought. AI-related investment
is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, and inflation in many goods and
services remains high. Liaison indicates that many firms are experiencing cost pressures and are
either increasing the prices of their goods and services in response or looking to do so. Inflation
is now forecast to remain elevated through much of 2027 and is not expected to reach the top of the
2–3 per cent target range until late 2027, around three quarters later than previously forecast. This
presents upside risks to inflation expectations; some measures are assessed to have risen lately.
The increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial
conditions. The economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly and the unemployment
rate has risen. The forecasts see growth in output slowing further over the coming year, which is
expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. Higher interest rates and
falls in housing prices and turnover are expected to weigh on growth in dwelling investment and
household consumption. On the other hand, growth in overall business investment is forecast to be
stronger in the near term, including data centre-related investment. Employment is expected to
continue to grow, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected in the August
forecasts.
There continue to be heightened uncertainties about the outlook for domestic economic activity and
inflation. The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is
higher and activity lower than forecast. Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward
pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. A period of prolonged uncertainty may
also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. To date, however, growth in Australia’s
major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has
outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict. In Australia, weak productivity growth
continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the extent and economic
effects of the downturn in the housing market.
Decision
Since the previous meeting, the data have confirmed that underlying inflation remains broadly based.
Capacity pressures appear a little tighter than previously estimated and there are indications that
higher fuel prices are being passed through to prices of other goods and services. Inflation is now
expected to remain above 3 per cent for the coming year and there is an increasing risk
that higher inflation expectations will become embedded.
The Board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high. Given the revised
inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in
financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target.
The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to
target. Accordingly, the Board will be attentive to the data and the evolving assessment of the
outlook and risks to guide its decisions. Monetary policy is well placed to respond to developments,
and the Board is focused on its mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.
Today’s policy decision was by majority: six members voted to increase the cash rate target by
25 basis points to 4.85 per cent; three members voted to leave the cash rate target
unchanged at 4.60 per cent.

CA.title: Bank of Canada raises the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2½%
CA.text:
The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%.
Since the July Monetary Policy Report , global economic activity has remained resilient, despite higher energy prices. In the United States, the economy continues to grow at a robust pace, supported by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area has been resilient and broad-based. After slowing in the second quarter, Chinese growth rebounded in the third quarter, owing to strength in exports and a pickup in fiscal spending. With persistently elevated oil prices and refinery margins, inflation has risen in most countries.
Given the ongoing resilience of the global economy, the Bank has revised up global GDP growth slightly to 3.1% in 2026, while growth in 2027 and 2028 remains unchanged from the July projection at 3.2%.
Global financial conditions have tightened since July. Advanced economy sovereign bond yields are higher. Equity and credit markets have been volatile due to uncertainty about the outlook for the AI sector. The Canadian dollar had weakened somewhat on US-dollar strength but has since recovered to around 71 cents – the same as assumed in the July Report.
Growth picked up in Canada through the middle of the year. GDP growth was 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to growth of about 2% in the third quarter. This is stronger than expected in the July Report. Consumer spending has been solid, even with slow population growth. Business investment rebounded, reflecting oil and gas sector activity and spending on machinery and equipment. Despite ongoing weakness in sectors affected by US tariffs, exports overall have strengthened, owing to robust US demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the changing trade environment. The unemployment rate has been around 6½% for several months. A broad set of indicators continue to point to some excess supply in the economy.
Owing to new US tariffs, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter of 2026, before picking up again in 2027. This rebound is supported by business investment, exports and fiscal measures. Consumption growth is expected to moderate and housing to remain relatively weak.
The Canadian economy is expected to grow 1% in 2026, and 2% in 2027 and 2028. This is a somewhat stronger overall growth projection than the July Report. This forecast is still subject to considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding Canada-US trade relations.
Given persistently high oil prices, CPI inflation has been around 3% since April and is expected to rise to about 3½% by the end of the year. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% in September and measures of core inflation remain close to 2%. But cost pressures are building, with high fuel prices raising the costs of production and transportation. Imported industrial and electronics input prices have also increased. While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, Bank surveys suggest cost pass-through will increase over the next year. Near-term household and business inflation expectations have risen, while longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.
The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices and increased pass-through adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection. CPI inflation is expected to average 3% in 2027, a percentage point above the July projection, then come down to 2% in the middle of 2028. The main sources of uncertainty around this forecast are developments in the Middle East and businesses’ responses to cost pressures.
In the outlook, inflation is higher and more persistent than in the July Report. Growth has picked up this year and is expected to recover further. Against this backdrop, Governing Council decided to increase the policy rate to reduce the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services. There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability.
Information note
The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is December 9, 2026. The Bank’s next Monetary Policy Report will be released on January 27, 2027.

CH.title: 2026-09-24 - Monetary policy assessment of 24 September 2026
CH.text:
Swiss National Bank leaves SNB policy rate unchanged at 0%
The Swiss National Bank is leaving the SNB policy rate unchanged at 0%. Banks' sight deposits held at the SNB will be remunerated at the SNB policy rate up to a certain threshold. The discount for sight deposits above this threshold is unchanged at 0.25 percentage points. The SNB is also willing to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary to ensure appropriate monetary conditions.
Inflation has risen further since June, primarily due to higher energy prices. Medium-term inflationary pressure has increased only slightly. Monetary policy is appropriate to keep inflation within the range consistent with price stability and supports economic development.
Inflation rose slightly, from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August. This increase was attributable to a rise in goods inflation, which was positive in August for the first time since May 2024. The rise in goods inflation was mainly driven by higher prices for oil products.
According to the conditional inflation forecast, inflation will continue to rise somewhat in the fourth quarter, before declining again over the course of 2027. This decrease is due to the fact that energy inflation, which is currently significantly elevated, is likely to decline again in the coming quarters. Thereafter, the conditional inflation forecast rises slightly.
The forecast for the shorter term is higher compared with the last monetary policy assessment. This is due to the higher-than-expected prices for oil products. For the medium term, too, the conditional inflation forecast is slightly higher than in the previous quarter, reflecting, among other things, the weakening of the Swiss franc. The conditional inflation forecast is within the range of price stability over the entire forecast horizon (cf. chart). It puts average annual inflation at 0.7% for 2026, 0.8% for 2027 and 0.8% for 2028 (cf. table). The forecast is based on the assumption that the SNB policy rate is 0% over the entire forecast horizon.
Global economic growth was stronger than expected in the second quarter. In many countries, inflation remains above central banks' targets, notably due to the higher energy prices. Key interest rates were raised both in the euro area and in the US.
In its baseline scenario, the SNB anticipates that growth in the global economy will be moderate over the coming quarters. Inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time.
The baseline scenario remains subject to high uncertainty, above all because of the situation in the Middle East. For example, energy prices could turn out to be significantly higher than expected. This would increase inflation further and significantly curb economic growth. In addition to the situation in the Middle East, the trade policy environment also remains uncertain.
Swiss GDP growth was exceptionally strong in the second quarter. An unusually robust performance in the chemicals/pharmaceuticals industry meant that GDP overstated the underlying growth momentum. However, even without this effect, growth was solid and broad-based. At the same time, capacity utilisation was below average, especially in manufacturing, while unemployment rose again somewhat through to early summer.
The SNB expects moderate growth for the coming quarters. Growth stimuli are likely to continue emanating from abroad. Moreover, monetary policy and the recent depreciation of the Swiss franc are having a supportive effect. For 2026 as a whole, the SNB currently expects growth of between 1.5% and 2%. The SNB continues to expect growth of around 1.5% for 2027.
The main risk to the economic outlook for Switzerland stems from developments in the global economy. In particular, the situation in the Middle East could deteriorate further and curb global economic activity more strongly. The trade policy environment and exchange rate developments also continue to be sources of uncertainty.
More detailed information on the monetary policy decision can be found in the introductory remarks by the Governing Board (available on the SNB website from 10 am on 24 September 2026).

GB.title: Bank rate increased to 4% - November 2026 Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes
GB.text:
Monetary Policy Summary, November 2026
At its meeting ending on 4 November 2026, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.
The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month. Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year. It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation.
While the direct effects of higher energy prices are clear, and will continue to feed into firm and household energy bills, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages. However, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, adding to the case for modestly tighter monetary policy.
Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path. The Committee will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour, and slack. The Committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2% target in the medium term.
Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee meeting ending on 4 November 2026
1: Before turning to its immediate policy decision, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) discussed key economic developments and its judgements around them, as well as its views on monetary policy strategy. The latest data and analysis underpinning these topics were set out in the accompanying November 2026 Monetary Policy Report .
The Committee’s discussions
2: The impact of protracted conflicts overseas on global energy prices remained the main source of uncertainty for the UK inflation outlook. The path for inflation was being shaped by the scale and duration of the energy and other global supply shocks, their knock-on impact on medium-term inflation through potential indirect and second-round effects, and the outlook for domestic activity and spare capacity. Monetary policy could not influence global energy prices, but was being set to ensure that the economic adjustment to them occurred in a way that achieved the 2% inflation target sustainably. The Committee would particularly need to guard against second-round effects that created inflation persistence, while considering any trade-off with weakness in economic activity.
3: Energy prices had remained sensitive to geopolitical news, and there had been significant further rises in spot and futures prices. The front-month Brent crude oil futures contract and the UK front-month natural gas futures contract averaged $108 per barrel and 216 pence per therm, respectively, over the 15 UK working days ending 27 October. These were 38% and 81% higher than at the time of the July Monetary Policy Report, and 5% and 27% above the respective 2026 Q4 futures-price assumptions in the July Report adverse scenario. Although a credible and sustained de-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East could lead prices to fall, continued periodic conflict, wider regional escalation or further damage to refining capacity could lead to persistently higher prices than embodied in current futures curves. There had also been a drawdown in energy supply buffers during 2026 which could amplify price pressures.
4: In the September UK CPI inflation outturn of 3.5%, direct energy effects had contributed around 1 percentage point, most of which was driven by fuels. These direct energy contributions were projected to build further in the next few quarters but then fall back, reflecting base effects and conditioning assumptions for wholesale energy prices based on futures curves that were downward sloping. There had been little sign so far of indirect effects from higher energy prices on other consumer goods prices, and in particular food inflation had remained lower than expected earlier in the year. Members discussed whether this was a sign of either diminished, or simply delayed, indirect effects. Although many firms were already facing higher prices for oil and refined products, some had not yet seen large rises in gas or electricity prices owing to hedging or longer-term fixed-price contracts. Agency intelligence suggested that many firms were also absorbing higher costs partly through lower profit margins.
5: The outlook for indirect effects on inflation would depend on the duration of the energy shock, and the extent to which firms could bear down on other costs or rebuild their margins in a stronger demand environment. The Committee judged that, for the most part, firms’ buffers would only prove temporary and that these cost pressures could eventually pass through into higher consumer prices if the energy shock persisted. There was, however, a risk that firms’ resilience to the energy shock would not last, instead resulting in weaker demand and then limiting firms’ pricing power.
6: The latest near-term inflation projection by Bank staff, which was based on energy prices averaged over the 15 UK working days to 27 October, was for headline CPI inflation to reach around 4½% in 2027 Q1, around 1¼ percentage points higher than at the time of the July Report, and around 5% in 2027 Q2.
7: Members noted that there was still limited evidence to date of second-round effects in wage and price-setting, although such effects typically only emerged with a longer lag and few indicators could yet be expected to reflect the impact of recent increases in energy prices. Forward-looking indicators of wage and price expectations from the DMP survey and Agents’ intelligence had moved little since September, though households and firms’ attentiveness was judged to be high, and there was a risk that outturns for wage settlements would turn out higher than firms’ current expectations if they were faced by outturns for headline inflation in the new year that were stronger than they had previously anticipated. Since second-round effects were likely to be state-dependent and the outlook for headline inflation had risen materially, the Committee judged that the risk of material second-round effects emerging had risen further since September and could remain a risk for some time.
8: The Committee continued to monitor wider global cost pressures, such as those triggered by adverse weather events and demand for AI components, although the potential impact of these risks on UK inflation was likely to be much smaller than for the energy shock and was not judged to have increased significantly since September. Despite the energy shock and these non-energy cost pressures, global activity growth had proved more resilient than expected, although it was expected to fall back next year.
9: The Committee had been briefed on the Budget on 28 October. The projections and scenarios in the November Report were conditioned on announced Government policy. The new policy measures in the Budget were expected to have a downward impact of ¼ percentage points on CPI inflation by 2027 Q2 and a small impact on activity. In absolute terms, the stance of fiscal policy remained likely to detract from growth over the medium term.
10: The Committee discussed the recent path of domestic activity and its implications for inflationary pressures. Since September, there had been further evidence of the resilience of activity despite higher energy prices. Momentum had been provided by the impact of global growth on UK exports, and some positive impact from the deployment of artificial intelligence. The impact of artificial intelligence on the UK economy was uncertain but was likely to affect both demand and supply. There was also some evidence that consumer demand had held up so far despite the impact of higher energy prices on real incomes, although the most recent consumer confidence reading suggested that this might not be maintained.
11: There was uncertainty around the extent to which the recent strength in GDP growth might persist, but on balance members judged that it was likely to fall back somewhat in the coming quarters. The outlook for growth would be sensitive to the behaviour of households and firms in the face of rises in energy costs and tighter financial conditions.
12: The increase in growth had been associated with signs of a stabilisation of the margin of slack in the economy, although members continued to differ in their views on how wide that margin was in absolute terms. It was likely that some slack would persist given the headwinds facing demand from households and firms. It would also be important to judge whether the factors boosting productivity growth over the past two years would lead to an ongoing boost to potential growth in the economy and, more broadly, the extent to which future growth would reduce spare capacity in the economy.
13: The Committee discussed the extent to which the underlying disinflation process that had been underway for some time before the Middle East conflict had proceeded as expected. Many measures of underlying inflation were no longer falling, and were judged to be somewhat above rates consistent with meeting the inflation target in the medium term. For some members, the news on domestic activity and underlying inflation was a signal that monetary policy had not been as restrictive as previously judged. For other members, it was premature to draw too much signal from outturns over the past few months, given the volatility of short-term economic indicators, uncertainty about the impact of technological change, and the difficulty of interpreting measures of underlying inflation completely independently of the energy shock.
14: Forward market interest rates had remained elevated compared with pre-conflict levels, and had continued to feed through to rates faced by some households and firms. Benchmark two-year mortgage rates had risen by nearly 50 basis points since the beginning of September. According to the Bank’s latest Market Participants Survey, the median expected path for Bank Rate had increased since September, reaching 4% in November and 4.25% in February, but had remained below the UK short-term interest rate curve.
15: Most members judged that the stance of monetary policy was still restrictive, although this judgement was sensitive to the choice of measure of the monetary stance, for example the extent to which it reflected expected inflation. The stance of monetary policy would also be experienced differently by different households and firms depending on their exposure to higher energy prices, technological change and interest rates. Members also noted that growth rates of lending to businesses had remained strong, although new mortgage approvals for households had been falling.
16: The Committee considered the updated central projection and the two scenarios that were set out in the November Report. The central projection assumed that there would be greater second-round effects on wage and price-setting than in the July Report owing to higher energy prices. The adverse scenario explored the risk of persistently higher energy prices and an additional mechanism for larger second-round effects which might occur as a consequence. The weaker demand scenario assumed that the recent resilience of domestic growth would falter and that widening spare capacity in the economy would limit the scope for second-round effects to emerge. These scenarios would all require different monetary policy responses if any of them were to materialise.
17: Taken together, the Committee judged that the risk of stronger inflationary pressure had increased further si

IN.title: Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) October 5 to 7, 2026
IN.text:
Monetary Policy Decisions
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held its 63rd meeting from October 5 to 7, 2026, under the chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India. The MPC members Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Prof. Ram Singh, Dr. Poonam Gupta and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya attended the meeting.
2. After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening.
Growth and Inflation Outlook
Global Outlook
3. Since the last MPC meeting in August 2026, the re-escalation of the conflict in West Asia and the consequent sharp volatility in crude oil prices has kept the global economy in a state of flux. Global growth has remained resilient. Acceleration of inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy. The US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September. The Fed commentary thereafter along with rate tightening by major systemically important central banks have reinforced expectations of higher global policy rates. Tighter global financial market conditions coupled with fiscal sustainability concerns in major economies are keeping global bond yields at record high levels. With a resolution of the West Asia conflict remaining elusive, significant downside risks to the global outlook remain, including further tightening of global financial conditions, continuing elevated AI-related asset valuations and high public debt.
Domestic Outlook
4. Notwithstanding these persisting global headwinds, the Indian economy has remained resilient. As per National Statistics Office (NSO) estimates, real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27 at 7.8 per cent was higher than expected. Strong private consumption and fixed investment, rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports supported growth. On the supply side, the manufacturing sector grew at a robust pace. Services sector activity strengthened further, owing to buoyant domestic and external demand.
5. In Q2, available high frequency indicators for July-August suggest sustained momentum in domestic economic activity. Domestic demand remains resilient and is well supported by robust external demand with merchandise exports registering double-digit growth.
6. Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty will continue to have some bearing on domestic economic activity. While energy prices and supply chain pressures have continued, their near-term trajectory remains uncertain amidst the lingering West Asia conflict. Their adverse impact is being contained with active diversification of supply sources. Deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Niño conditions pose risks to agriculture sector’s outlook and rural demand, although healthy buffer of foodgrains and proactive policy interventions by the government are expected to mitigate the impact. Furthermore, continuing momentum in services and broadly stable employment conditions are likely to support urban demand. Strong capacity utilisation, robust credit flows and the government’s thrust on infrastructure are expected to sustain investment activity. While services exports are expected to remain buoyant, bilateral trade agreements should boost merchandise exports.
7. Taking all these factors into consideration, real GDP growth for 2026-27 is projected at 7.1 per cent, with Q2 at 7.2 per cent; Q3 at 6.9 per cent and Q4 at 6.8 per cent. Real GDP growth for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 7.1 per cent. The risks are evenly balanced ( Chart 1 ).
8. CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July. While the increase has been predominantly on account of higher inflation in food and fuel groups, core inflation has also picked up indicating some signs of widening price pressures. Food price increases have become more broad based along with notable spikes in certain items such as sugar and onion. The uptick in fuel inflation in August largely reflected unfavourable base effects. Core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent and core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August. The weighted share of items in headline CPI recording inflation above 4 per cent increased steadily to about 37 per cent in August.
9. The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from supply side on account of the deficient monsoon, ongoing El Niño conditions and high energy and other commodity prices, the pass through of which is still continuing. Considering all factors, CPI inflation is projected to be 5.2 per cent for 2026-27 with Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent ( Chart 2 ). Inflation for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 5.6 per cent with risks being evenly balanced. Core inflation is projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27.
Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions
10. The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong. The economic momentum remains broad-based. The economy is expected to remain resilient.
11. In the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative.
12. As regards supply side inflation, monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are only limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour.
13. Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist.
14. Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. It only signals that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses.
15. Two members - Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh - were of the view that the stance be retained at neutral.
16. The MPC remains committed to its price stability mandate and will endeavour to progressively align inflation with its target.
17. The minutes of the MPC’s meeting will be published on October 21, 2026.
18. The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026.
(Brij Raj)
Chief General Manager

JP.title: Statement on Monetary Policy
JP.text:
October 30, 2026
Bank of Japan
Statement on Monetary Policy
1. Guideline for money market operations (an 8-1 majority vote)
[Note]
At the Monetary Policy Meeting (MPM) held today, the Policy Board of the Bank of Japan
decided to set the following guideline for money market operations for the intermeeting period:
The Bank will encourage the uncollateralized overnight call rate to remain at around 1.25
percent.
2. Change in the pace of sales of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) (a unanimous vote)
At the MPM held in September 2025, the Bank, drawing on its experience of the smooth
conduct of sales of the "stocks purchased from financial institutions" through July 2025,
decided to sell its ETF holdings for the time being at a scale generally equivalent to that of the
sales of the "stocks purchased from financial institutions" (the sales amount accounted for
about 0.05 percent of the trading value in the market at the time), and set the pace of sales at
about 330 billion yen per year (on a book value basis).
The Bank started its sales of ETFs in January 2026, and has been conducting these sales
smoothly while avoiding a major impact on the market. Meanwhile, the trading value in the
stock market has been expanding. Given these developments, at the MPM held today, the Bank
decided to sell its ETF holdings at a scale of about 0.1 percent of the trading value in the market,
and set the pace of sales at about 860 billion yen per year (on a book value basis).
1,2,3,4
1
The pace of sales is calculated using the trading value in the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market from
January to September 2026 and the market-to-book ratio of the ETFs sold by the Bank during the same period.
If the annual sales amount is converted to market value using the same ratio, it would be about 2,460 billion
yen.
2
The change will be implemented in January 2027.
3
A temporary adjustment in the sales amount or a suspension of sales may be made within the range of the
annual sales pace in response to changes in financial market conditions. (This remains the same as before.)
4
The pace of sales of Japan real estate investment trusts (J-REITs) will remain at about 5 billion yen per
year (on a book value basis).
2
[Note]
Voting for the action: UEDA Kazuo, HIMINO Ryozo, UCHIDA Shinichi, TAMURA Naoki, KOEDA
Junko, MASU Kazuyuki, ASADA Toichiro, and SATO Ayano. Voting against the action: TAKATA
Hajime. Takata Hajime considered that, with underlying CPI inflation having reached the price stability
target, the situation had shifted to a new phase in which the Bank needs to step up the pace of bringing
the policy interest rate closer to the neutral interest rate so that it could make nimble responses. He
proposed that the Bank set the guideline for money market operations as follows: the Bank would
encourage the uncollateralized overnight call rate to remain at around 1.5 percent. The proposal was
defeated by a majority vote.

NO.title: Policy rate kept unchanged at 4.5 percent
NO.text:
Press release
Policy rate kept unchanged at 4.5 percent
Norges Bank’s Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee decided to keep the policy rate unchanged at 4.5% at its meeting on 4 November.
“Inflation is too high. It will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time, and we are prepared to raise the policy rate if needed to bring inflation down to target within a reasonable time horizon ”, says Governor Ida Wolden Bache.
Inflation has been above target for several years. Capacity utilisation in the Norwegian economy has declined and appears to be slightly below a normal level. At the monetary policy meeting in September, the policy rate was raised to 4.5%, and the Committee judged that it would likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time. Since September, the Committee has noted the following:
The conflicts in the Middle East are still creating substantial uncertainty about the inflation outlook. Oil spot prices have fallen, but futures prices have increased somewhat. Spot and futures prices for gas and electricity have moved up. Indicators of external price impulses to Norwegian imported goods have risen further as expected. The krone has appreciated and is stronger than assumed. In Norway, inflation has evolved broadly as projected. Twelve-month CPI inflation was 3.4% in September, while CPI inflation adjusted for tax changes and excluding energy products (CPI-ATE) was 3.0%. Domestically produced goods and services inflation remains elevated and has been higher than projected in the September Report .
Both LFS data and registered unemployment statistics indicate little change in unemployment in recent months. Registered unemployment has been a bit lower than projected. Preliminary figures for the number of salaried employees indicate that employment has increased a little more than expected.
The Committee judges that a restrictive monetary policy is still needed to bring inflation down to target within a reasonable time horizon. Inflation remains markedly above target, and the rapid rise in business costs in recent years will likely contribute to keeping inflation elevated ahead. High inflation over time can make inflation stickier and harder to bring down again. At the same time, the Committee does not want to restrict the economy more than needed.
The Committee has not received information indicating that the outlook for the Norwegian economy has changed materially since its monetary policy meeting in September. The Committee’s current assessment of the outlook implies that it will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time. The Committee is prepared to raise the policy rate if warranted by the inflation outlook.
The future path of the policy rate will depend on how the economy evolves. The Committee will have received more information about economic developments ahead of its next monetary policy meeting in December, when new forecasts will also be presented.
New forecasts were not prepared for this meeting. Monetary Policy Report 4/26 will be published together with the policy rate decision on 17 December 2026.

SE.title: Policy rate raised to 2 per cent
SE.text:
The Executive Board has therefore decided to raise the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2 per cent. If the outlook for inflation and economic activity holds, it is likely that the policy rate will be raised further in the coming year, in line with the policy rate forecast in September.

04/11/2026
Global inflationary pressures remain elevated due to supply disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East. Energy prices have risen further and inflation abroad has increased. In Sweden, CPIF inflation was 1.5 per cent in September, in line with the Riksbank's latest forecast. Inflation is still being held back by direct effects of temporary fiscal policy measures. Excluding these, CPIF inflation was 3 per cent. The measure that currently best reflects the more underlying inflation, which also excludes energy prices, amounted to 1.6 per cent. This was slightly lower than expected. At the same time, indicators point to cost pressures still being above normal. According to preliminary statistics, GDP increased during the third quarter and employment rose, both in line with the forecast. Sentiment among households declined in October, but among companies it rose further.
Overall, recent developments have largely been in line with the Riksbank's forecast, which implies that economic conditions are strengthening further and will become normal next year. The labour market is also expected to continue to improve. The combination of stronger economic activity, cost increases due to supply disruptions and a weaker krona this year is expected to contribute to both CPIF inflation and underlying inflation rising above 2 per cent next year.
The Riksbank has therefore decided to raise the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2 per cent. If the outlook for inflation and economic activity holds, the Riksbank assesses that it is likely that the policy rate will be raised further in the coming year, in line with the policy rate forecast in September. With this monetary policy, inflation is expected to stabilise around the target of 2 per cent after a while.
There are several risks that could affect the outlook. The causes of supply disruptions remain, which increases the risk that inflation will be too high. The upturn in economic activity has gained momentum and it cannot be ruled out that the economy will grow faster than expected. Despite signs of improvement, there is nevertheless uncertainty regarding the strength of the recovery in the labour market. There are also risks of weaker demand linked to the global economy, such as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns about AI investments, and weak public finances in certain countries. As always, the Riksbank evaluates the outlook for inflation and economic activity in the light of new information and adjusts monetary policy accordingly.
The decision on the policy rate will apply from 11 November 2026. The minutes from the Executive Board’s monetary policy meeting will be published on
10 November 2026. A press conference with Governor Erik Thedéen, and Åsa Olli Segendorf, Head of the Monetary Policy Department, will be held today at 11.00 at the Riksbank. Press cards or the equivalent are required to participate. Advance registration is required, to press officer Susanne Meyer, susanne.meyer@riksbank.se no later than 10.00 on 4 November 2026. The press conference will be broadcast live on riksbank.se.
About the Monetary Policy Update
A Monetary Policy Update is published in connection with the policy rate decision, containing the Executive Board's assessment of how new information affects economic prospects and monetary policy. The update does not contain any new forecasts. The next Monetary Policy Report containing forecasts will be published on 16 December 2026.

US.title: Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
US.text:
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

XM.title: Monetary policy decisions
XM.text:
The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage. The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. Financing conditions have tightened since the Governing Council’s last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. The Governing Council is committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term.
The Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. It will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, the Governing Council’s interest rate decisions will be based on its assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.
Key ECB interest rates
The interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will remain unchanged at 2.50%, 2.65% and 2.90% respectively.
Asset purchase programme (APP) and pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP)
The APP and PEPP portfolios are declining at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests the principal payments from maturing securities.
***
The Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments within its mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission. Moreover, the Transmission Protection Instrument is available to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across all euro area countries, thus allowing the Governing Council to more effectively deliver on its price stability mandate.
The President of the ECB will comment on the considerations underlying these decisions at a press conference starting at 14:45 CET today.
